thread.title: U.S. Stocks Run Ahead As Investors Pass On Foreign Equity Plays

author: NANCY GONDO
title: U.S. Stocks Run Ahead As Investors Pass On Foreign Equity Plays
text:
Foreign equity ETFs continue to lag U.S. stocks this year as investors favor domestic plays and pull money out of many international funds.
X None of the top 13 foreign ETFs outperformed the S&P 500 this year through Wednesday, according to Morningstar Direct. Furthermore, none of the funds' average annual returns over the past three and five years have beaten the S&P index.
Top honors went to iShares MSCI Saudi Arabia ( KSA ), with a 9.5% year-to-date return. The $249.4 million fund came closest to the S&P 500's 9.8% year to date gain. Since KSA will be marking its third anniversary later this month, it doesn't yet have a three-year average figure. It had rallied as much as 22% through its June 5 high.
The ETF tracks the MSCI Saudi Arabia IMI 25/50 Index. Financials accounted for the biggest sector weighting as of Wednesday at nearly 41% of assets. Materials was next at 34%, followed by roughly 6% each in telecommunications and consumer staples. Its top five holdings — Saudi Basic Industries, Al Rajhi Bank, National Commercial Bank, Saudi Telecom and Samba Financial Group — made up 46% of the 72-stock portfolio.
Up next is Global X MSCI Norway ( NORW ), with an 8% year-to-date return. The $167.1 million fund, which tracks the MSCI Norway IMI 25/50 Index, posted respective average annual returns of 14% and 1.9% over the past three and five years. The S&P 500 has returned 17.1% and 14.2% for those same periods. NORW's top five holdings — energy company Equinor ( EQNR ), financial services group DNB, telecom Telenor, seafood company Marine Harvest and chemicals firm Yara International — represented nearly 50% of the 61-stock portfolio.
In third place: iShares Global 100 ( IOO ) with a 5.3% gain for the year. The $1.9 billion fund tracks the S&P Global 100, which measures the performance of 100 large-cap global stocks. The U.S. accounted for 66% of assets as of Wednesday, the U.K. 9.5%, and France, Switzerland and Germany about 5% each. Japan, Korea, the Netherlands and Spain took smaller positions.
The top five holdings are all U.S. household names: Apple ( AAPL ), Microsoft ( MSFT ), Amazon ( AMZN ), JPMorgan ( JPM ) and Johnson & Johnson ( JNJ ). They made up nearly 29% of total assets.
U.S. equity ETFs outperformed their foreign counterparts in August, according to State Street Global Advisors' latest U.S. ETF Flash Flows Report.
Domestic equity ETFs saw $19.7 billion in inflows last month, bringing the year-to-date total to $111.5 billion. Meantime, European regional funds suffered outflows for the sixth month in a row. Emerging markets, which have been hit hard, saw their biggest inflows since January. But U.S. funds still sharply outperformed emerging markets.
'Bo Knows' "On a regional basis, the U.S. continues to be the 'quick slant' play call, outperforming developed and emerging markets by 5.5% and 6.2% in August, respectively," Matthew Bartolini, head of SPDR Americas Research at SSGA, said in the report. "A stronger U.S. dollar, protectionist trade policies and a Cleveland Browns-like handling of the Brexit negotiations have forced investors to sidestep developed ex-U.S. and emerging markets like Bo Jackson juking a defender in the open field."
U.S. funds led geographical flows by taking in nearly $16 billion in August, pushing the year-to-date total to $76.8 billion. Global stock funds saw an incremental increase of $293 million for a YTD total of $13.4 billion. International-developed and emerging markets saw a respective $1.8 billion and $1.5 billion in inflows for year-to-date totals of $29.5 billion and $7.6 billion.
Bartolini thinks the flows into emerging markets may be a value play, since those stocks are trading at a steeper-than-usual discount to U.S. equities. Based on price-to-book ratios, he says, emerging markets stocks now trade at a 54% discount vs. a 25-year median discount of 45%.

"Outside the U.S., regional funds continue to be sent to the bench, largely as a result of the play by the Europeans," Bartolini wrote. "Strategies focusing on either the eurozone or the European region have now witnessed six consecutive months of outflows. This represents the longest such stretch since Brexit and a shedding of nearly 13% of their asset base in 2018."
